**REFLEX**

**Final Project Documentation**

Delivery coordination for small Kenyan retailers

| Document purposeThis expanded document consolidates the supplied Reflex architecture, final build documentation, executive narrative, ERD, workflows, trade-offs, demonstration flow, limitations, and roadmap into one rounded project record. It is intended to explain not only what was built, but how the pieces fit together and why the final design looks the way it does. |
| :---- |

**Final build source of truth: Lovable Cloud / Supabase**

**1\. Project Overview**  
Reflex is a delivery-coordination system designed around a simple operational problem: small retailers need a reliable way to create, assign, track, and confirm deliveries without depending on fragmented WhatsApp conversations and phone calls.

The supplied executive narrative describes Reflex as a shared source of truth for a delivery. Instead of information being passed from retailer to dispatcher to rider through separate conversations, the delivery exists as one record that progresses through visible states.

| Core propositionReflex turns informal delivery coordination into one visible, trackable, and auditable workflow. |
| :---- |

**1.1 Final Build at a Glance**

| Area | Final position |
| :---- | :---- |
| Application | One responsive React \+ Tailwind web application |
| Backend | Lovable Cloud / Supabase |
| Database | PostgreSQL |
| Access control | Supabase Row-Level Security |
| Real-time | Supabase Realtime using postgres\_changes |
| Core tables | retailers, profiles, delivery\_requests, assignments, status\_updates |
| Delivery states | Requested, Assigned, Picked Up, Delivered |
| Delivery confirmation | Six-character confirmation code |
| Primary user roles | Retailer staff, dispatcher, rider |

**2\. Business and Operational Problem**  
The case study focuses on small Kenyan retailers, including electronics shops, pharmacies, and hardware stores. Their delivery coordination is described as being handled through WhatsApp and phone calls.

**2.1 Problems Created by the Existing Process**

| Problem | Operational consequence | Reflex response |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| No assignment record | It may be unclear who is responsible for a delivery. | Assignments are stored against the delivery request. |
| No status visibility | Retailers must ask for updates rather than seeing progress directly. | Current delivery status is visible and synchronized. |
| No proof of delivery | A delivery being 'done' may rely on a verbal claim. | The rider enters a confirmation code to complete delivery. |

**2.2 Why a Shared Record Matters**  
The system is intentionally centered on the delivery request as the shared unit of work. Retailer staff create it, dispatchers act on it, riders execute it, and the status history records how it progressed.

**3\. Project Goals and Scope**

**3.1 Core Goals**

* Provide a single record for each delivery request.  
* Allow retailer staff to create delivery requests with the required customer and item information.  
* Allow dispatchers to see open requests and assign riders.  
* Allow riders to see their assigned deliveries and update delivery status.  
* Provide live status visibility to permitted users.  
* Provide a confirmation step before a delivery becomes Delivered.  
* Preserve status history as an audit trail.  
* Enforce role-based access at the database layer.  
  **3.2 Deliberate MVP Boundaries**  
  The supplied materials show that the team deliberately prioritized the core delivery workflow over features that would add significant engineering complexity during the sprint.  
* Rider assignment is manual rather than automatically optimized.  
* Delivery confirmation uses a typed six-character code rather than camera QR scanning.  
* The backend is managed through Supabase rather than a custom Node.js API.  
* The rider workflow does not currently provide offline-first synchronization.

**4\. Users and Responsibilities**

| Persona | Primary responsibility | System interaction |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Retailer staff | Create and monitor delivery requests | Creates requests and sees status progression for their retailer. |
| Dispatcher | Coordinate open requests and assign riders | Views requests and rider profiles; creates assignments. |
| Rider | Execute assigned deliveries | Views assigned requests, marks Picked Up, and confirms Delivered using the code. |

**4.1 Role Boundaries**  
The application uses role-based access so the same application codebase can support all three personas while each login receives an appropriate view and database permissions.

**5\. Solution Overview**  
Reflex replaces a fragmented conversation-based process with a shared state-based workflow. Each delivery begins as Requested and progresses through assignment, pickup, and delivery confirmation.

**5.1 End-to-End Conceptual Flow**  
**RETAILER → REQUESTED → DISPATCHER ASSIGNS → RIDER PICKS UP → CODE CONFIRMED → DELIVERED**

**5.2 Shared Source of Truth**  
The executive deck describes the central design principle as one shared source of truth rather than a group chat. The delivery record carries the information through the workflow, so participants do not need to repeatedly re-enter or explain the same delivery details.

**6\. Functional Workflow**

**6.1 Retailer Request Creation**

* Retailer staff logs in.  
* Retailer opens New Delivery.  
* Retailer enters customer name, customer phone, address, and item description.  
* Retailer submits the request.  
* The request is stored in delivery\_requests with Requested status.  
* A confirmation code is generated for the request.  
  **6.2 Dispatcher Assignment**  
* Dispatcher views open delivery requests.  
* Dispatcher selects an available rider.  
* An assignment is inserted into assignments.  
* The request moves to Assigned.  
* The rider's availability changes to busy.  
  **6.3 Rider Execution**  
* Rider sees the assigned delivery.  
* Rider marks the request Picked Up.  
* A status\_updates record is created.  
* At drop-off, the rider enters the request's confirmation code.  
* Successful confirmation moves the request to Delivered.  
* The rider's availability changes back to available.  
  **6.4 Status History**  
  Every transition is written to the status\_updates table as a new record. This means the history is retained instead of being overwritten each time the current status changes.

**7\. Functional Requirements**

| ID | Requirement | Implemented position |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| FR-01 | Create a delivery request | Retailer staff creates delivery\_requests records. |
| FR-02 | Capture customer and item details | Customer name, phone, address and item description are stored. |
| FR-03 | Track delivery status | Request status follows Requested → Assigned → PickedUp → Delivered. |
| FR-04 | Assign a rider | Dispatcher inserts an assignment linking request and rider. |
| FR-05 | Restrict rider visibility | Rider access is limited to assigned delivery requests through RLS. |
| FR-06 | Update delivery status | Rider can update the status of assigned requests. |
| FR-07 | Confirm delivery | Rider enters a six-character confirmation code at drop-off. |
| FR-08 | Keep status history | Each transition creates a status\_updates record. |
| FR-09 | Synchronize changes | Supabase Realtime pushes permitted changes to open sessions. |
| FR-10 | Protect data by role | RLS policies enforce database-level access boundaries. |

**8\. Final Architecture**  
The final architecture is a single responsive web application backed by Supabase services. The supplied final documentation states that the final build supersedes the architecture section of the earlier design.

**8.1 Architecture Layers**

| Layer | Component | Role |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Presentation | React \+ Tailwind | Provides retailer, dispatcher, and rider dashboards in one responsive application. |
| Application backend | Lovable Cloud / Supabase | Provides authentication, database connectivity, access control, and real-time capabilities. |
| Data | PostgreSQL | Stores retailers, profiles, delivery requests, assignments and status history. |
| Authorization | Supabase RLS | Determines what each role can query and modify at the database layer. |
| Real-time | Supabase Realtime | Pushes relevant database changes to permitted open sessions. |

**8.2 Why One Application?**  
A single codebase allows the same product to support all three roles. The user's role determines what that account can see and do, rather than requiring separate applications for retailer staff, dispatchers, and riders.

**9\. Technology Stack and Rationale**

| Technology | Use | Rationale in supplied project material |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| React | Client application | Supports the single responsive application for the three roles. |
| Tailwind | Interface styling | Used with React for the responsive web application. |
| Lovable Cloud / Supabase | Managed backend platform | Provides authentication, database access, RLS and real-time synchronization without building a custom API during the sprint. |
| PostgreSQL | Database | Provides a relational structure and supports schema constraints such as unique assignments per request. |
| Supabase Realtime | Live updates | Uses postgres\_changes to push relevant changes without polling. |

**9.1 Architecture Decision Principle**  
The final technology choices are framed around sprint practicality: use managed capabilities where they can provide working authentication, security and synchronization without spending most of the sprint implementing equivalent infrastructure from scratch.

**10\. Database and Data Model**  
The final build contains five application tables. Supabase auth.users remains the authentication source; profiles references it and supplies the application's role and profile information.

| Table | Key fields | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| retailers | id, shop\_name, phone, address | Represents the retailer/shop. The supplied build is seeded with one demo retailer. |
| profiles | id, role, name, phone, retailer\_id, availability | Represents authenticated application users and their role. |
| delivery\_requests | id, retailer\_id, created\_by, customer\_name, customer\_phone, address, item\_description, status, confirmation\_code, created\_at | Core delivery record. |
| assignments | id, request\_id, rider\_id, assigned\_by, assigned\_at | Connects a request to a rider and records who assigned it. |
| status\_updates | id, request\_id, status, updated\_by, created\_at | Append-only transition history and audit trail. |

**10.1 Important Constraints**

* assignments.request\_id is unique, enforcing one active assignment per request at the schema level.  
* profiles.id references Supabase auth.users.  
* delivery\_requests has foreign-key relationships to the retailer and creator profile.  
* assignments references the rider and assigning profile.  
* status\_updates references the request and the profile that performed the update.

**11\. Security and Access Control**  
Security is a core part of the final architecture. The supplied documentation explicitly states that access control is enforced at the database layer rather than relying only on the interface.

| Role | Can see | Can write |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Retailer staff | Delivery requests belonging to their retailer\_id | Create delivery requests for their retailer |
| Dispatcher | All delivery requests and rider profiles | Insert assignments and update request status to Assigned |
| Rider | Delivery requests assigned to that rider | Update status on their own assigned requests |

**11.1 Why Database-Level Enforcement Matters**  
The final documentation emphasizes that hiding an item in the interface is not the security boundary. RLS policies restrict what the authenticated session can actually retrieve or change. The supplied design specifically states that a rider's session cannot query another rider's assignments.

**12\. Real-Time Synchronization**  
Reflex uses Supabase Realtime with postgres\_changes subscriptions. When an authorized database change occurs, permitted open sessions can receive the change without manually refreshing the page.

**12.1 Example**

* Retailer creates a delivery request.  
* Dispatcher's open session receives the new request.  
* Dispatcher assigns a rider.  
* Retailer's open session receives the Assigned status.  
* Rider's open session receives the assignment.  
* Rider changes status to Picked Up.  
* The retailer can receive that status change live.  
* After code confirmation, Delivered is synchronized and the full history can be displayed.  
  **12.2 Why No Polling?**  
  The final build replaced the earlier proposal of Socket.io plus a polling fallback with Supabase Realtime. The supplied documentation describes this as a deliberate simplification that avoids custom reconnect logic and periodic polling.

**13\. Assignment and Status Logic**

**13.1 Assignment Logic**  
Assignment is intentionally dispatcher-controlled. The dispatcher chooses an available rider rather than relying on an automated routing or matching algorithm.

**13.2 Status Transition Logic**

| Current stage | Action | Result |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Requested | Dispatcher assigns rider | Assigned |
| Assigned | Rider picks up delivery | PickedUp |
| PickedUp | Rider enters valid confirmation code | Delivered |

**13.3 Availability Logic**  
When a dispatcher assigns a rider, the rider's availability is changed to busy. When the rider completes delivery through the confirmation step, availability changes back to available.

**14\. Delivery Confirmation and Audit Trail**

**14.1 Confirmation Code**  
The original design called for camera-based QR confirmation. The final build instead generates a six-character confirmation code for the request. The rider enters the code at drop-off before the request can be completed as Delivered.

**14.2 Audit Trail**  
The current status field represents the latest state, while status\_updates preserves the sequence of transitions. The supplied final documentation describes status\_updates as append-only: a new row is created for each transition rather than overwriting history.

| Design principleThe current state tells you where the delivery is now; the status history tells you how it got there. |
| :---- |

**15\. Evolution from Original Design**  
The supplied final documentation explicitly records several changes from the original proposal. These changes should be presented as documented trade-offs rather than unexplained inconsistencies.

| Area | Original design | Final build | Reason recorded by team |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Backend | Custom Node.js \+ Express API | Lovable Cloud / Supabase | Managed authentication, access control and synchronization were available without hand-building and securing an API during the sprint. |
| Real-time | Socket.io \+ 30s polling fallback | Supabase Realtime | Built-in real-time behavior avoided custom reconnect and polling logic. |
| Confirmation | Camera QR scan | Six-character typed code | Camera permissions and scan libraries were considered fragile for a one-pass sprint build. |
| User model | Generic User \+ separate Rider | Single profiles table with role | Supabase reserves users for auth; profiles gives each persona a first-class application account. |

**16\. Trade-offs and Limitations**  
The team is expected to identify weaknesses before the panel does. The supplied material provides four concrete trade-offs.

**16.1 Manual Rider Assignment**  
Simplification: the dispatcher selects riders manually; there is no route optimization or automatic matching.

Why accepted: the documented target is a handful of shops and well under 50 deliveries per day per shop, where dispatcher local knowledge is considered more useful than an untuned algorithm.

Future: add proximity-based suggestions using last known rider location while keeping the dispatcher in control.

**16.2 Typed Code Instead of QR**  
Simplification: the rider types a six-character code instead of scanning a QR code.

Why accepted: camera permissions and scanning libraries were considered fragile to guarantee in the sprint.

Future: add camera QR scanning as an alternative once the core flow is stable.

**16.3 Managed Backend**  
Simplification: no custom Node.js API server.

Why accepted: Supabase provides authentication, RLS and real-time synchronization without requiring the team to build and secure equivalent infrastructure in the sprint.

Future: move genuinely custom business logic, such as complex assignment rules or notifications, into Supabase Edge Functions as complexity grows.

**16.4 No Offline Rider Mode**  
Simplification: rider status updates require a live connection.

Why accepted: offline-first synchronization and conflict resolution were treated as a separate engineering project that would have crowded out the core flow.

Future: queue status updates locally and replay them in order after connectivity returns.

**17\. Edge Cases and Failure Considerations**  
The following are grounded in the supplied trade-offs and architecture. They are also useful areas for live questioning.

| Scenario | Current handling/limitation | Potential future response |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Rider is offline | Current status update requires a live connection. | Local queue and ordered replay after reconnection. |
| Automated assignment needed | Current system uses manual dispatcher selection. | Proximity-based recommendations. |
| QR confirmation required | Current system uses typed confirmation code. | Add QR as an additional confirmation method. |
| More complex business rules | Core system uses managed Supabase services. | Use Edge Functions for custom logic. |
| Duplicate assignment for same request | assignments. request\_id is unique. | Database constraint prevents multiple active assignment rows for a request. |

Other hypothetical failures may be raised by the panel. Where the supplied materials do not specify a current implementation, the team should avoid claiming that the system handles the case. A strong answer is to state the current limitation and explain how it would be investigated or addressed.

**18\. Demonstration Plan**  
The supplied demo script recommends three separate logged-in sessions, not merely three tabs in one browser. The purpose is to demonstrate actual live synchronization between independent sessions.

| Step | Actor | Demo action | Message / evidence |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | Retailer | Create a delivery with customer and item details. | Demonstrates a real delivery\_requests insert. |
| 2 | Dispatcher | Observe request appear without refresh and assign rider. | Demonstrates Realtime and assignment. |
| 3 | Retailer | Observe status change to Assigned. | Demonstrates synchronization back to retailer. |
| 4 | Rider | See assignment and mark Picked Up. | Demonstrates rider workflow. |
| 5 | Rider | Enter confirmation code and confirm delivery. | Demonstrates proof-of-delivery step. |
| 6 | Retailer | Open request and show full status history. | Demonstrates append-only audit trail. |

**18.1 Demo Discipline**

* Use separate authenticated sessions.  
* Know the exact sequence before presenting.  
* Do not introduce untested features during the demo.  
* Show the state change rather than only describing it.  
* Be ready to explain what is real data versus what is presentation framing.

**20\. Roadmap**

| Phase | Scope | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Phase 1 — Built | Log delivery, assign rider, update status, confirmation by code, real-time sync. | Establish the core trackable delivery workflow. |
| Phase 2 — Next | Camera QR scanning, rider offline queue, and  proximity-based assignment suggestions. | Improve convenience, resilience and dispatch efficiency. |
| Phase 3 — Later | Dispute resolution and delivery analytics. | Extend operational visibility and support more advanced workflows. |

**21\. Cross-Examination Preparation**  
The strongest answers should follow State → Context → Evidence. The following questions are directly aligned with the supplied architecture and trade-offs.

| Question | Key point to defend |
| :---- | :---- |
| Why Supabase instead of a custom API? | Managed authentication, RLS and Realtime reduced sprint implementation and security overhead. |
| Why React \+ Tailwind? | One responsive codebase supports all three role-based dashboards. |
| Why PostgreSQL? | Relational structure fits users, retailers, requests, assignments and status history; schema constraints can enforce important relationships. |
| How do you protect rider data? | RLS is enforced at the database layer and rider visibility is restricted to assigned requests. |
| Why manual assignment? | The documented target volume is small and dispatcher local knowledge is acceptable at MVP scale. |
| Why not QR? | Typed code was chosen as a more reliable sprint implementation; QR is on the roadmap. |
| What happens offline? | The current rider workflow requires live connectivity; offline queueing is a future enhancement. |
| How is delivery history preserved? | status\_updates is append-only, creating an audit trail. |
| How do you prevent two assignments for one request? | assignments.request\_id has a unique constraint. |
| What is the weakest part of the build? | Choose one documented trade-off and explain why it was accepted and how it would be improved. |
| What would you build next? | Use the roadmap: QR, offline queue, proximity suggestions, then dispute resolution and analytics. |

**21.1 Candor Rule**  
If a question reaches beyond the current build, the team should not invent an implementation. State what is known, explain the current limitation, and describe how the team would investigate or implement the missing capability.

**22\. Conclusion**  
Reflex provides a focused solution to a specific operational problem: delivery coordination that is currently fragmented across WhatsApp and phone calls. The final build turns the delivery into a structured record with defined roles, visible states, rider assignment, live synchronization, delivery confirmation, and an audit trail.

The architecture is intentionally sized for the sprint. React and Tailwind provide a single responsive client; Lovable Cloud / Supabase provides managed backend capabilities; PostgreSQL stores the relational data; RLS provides database-level access control; and Supabase Realtime provides live updates.

The system is not presented as complete or perfectly scalable. Its documented limitations—manual assignment, typed confirmation, managed backend dependence, and no offline rider mode—are part of the design story. The roadmap shows how those limitations can be addressed as requirements and scale increase.

| Final takeawayReflex creates one shared, trackable, and auditable delivery workflow for retailer staff, dispatchers and riders. |
